title: Refund approval: paying back a customer
goal: Understand how a planned local tool turns a sample refund request into an approved, simulated payout, and why each safeguard is needed.

includes: The planned journey from a refund request and policy to a simulated payout
The safeguards listed in the refund scope document
excludes: Any running code: none exists yet, so this board describes intentions, not verified behavior
Real payouts, real customer data, login, scheduling, and deployment

groups.label: Team screens
groups.description: What the team member sees and acts on.

groups.label: Refund logic
groups.description: Decisions the app makes from the inputs.

groups.label: Local storage
groups.description: Data that must survive a restart.

components.label: Refund request
components.summary: A sample $100 refund request and the policy that the user enters.
components.explanation: Everything starts here. The request is a **sample**, and the policy comes from the user, not from built-in rules.
inputs: Request details typed or loaded by the user
Refund policy typed by the user
outputs: Request and policy for the policy check

components.label: Spending limit
components.summary: An amount the user sets by hand, so the same request gives the same result every time.
inputs: A limit chosen by the user

components.label: Policy check
components.summary: Compares the request with the policy and the limit, and proposes a payout if allowed.
components.explanation: The policy check only *proposes*. It does not pay anything, and it never changes the request or the policy.
outputs: A proposed payout, or no payout

components.label: Payout preview
components.summary: Shows the exact amount and the exact account before anything can happen.
components.explanation: The user must see what would be paid, to the cent. Approval of a vague summary would not protect anyone.
outputs: Exact amount and account shown to the user

components.label: Manager approval
components.summary: The manager approves or rejects one specific version of the proposed payout.
components.explanation: Approval belongs to **one version** of the payout. If the amount or account changes, the old approval no longer counts.

components.label: Simulated payout
components.summary: Pretends to pay an approved refund and shows the result. No money moves.
components.explanation:
The payout must be blocked when the refund is:

- not approved
- rejected
- already paid

components.label: Payout ledger
components.summary: Local file storage that keeps decisions and payout results across an app restart.
components.explanation: The safeguards only work if the app still remembers them after a restart. Otherwise a restart could allow a second payout.

relationships.label: approved payout version
relationships.explanation: Only an approval of the current version can start a simulated payout.

scenarios.title: Approve and pay
scenarios.summary: The normal path from a refund request to a simulated payout.

steps.caption: The user enters the sample request and a policy, and sets a spending limit above the amount.
The policy check finds that the policy allows the refund and proposes a payout.
The preview shows the exact amount and account.
The manager approves this version, and the decision is saved.
The simulated payout runs and its result is saved.
The preview shows the proposed payout.
The manager rejects it. The rejection is saved.
No simulated payout is allowed for a rejected refund.
The user edits the amount. This makes a new version of the payout.
The earlier approval was for the old version, so the payout is blocked until the manager approves the new one.
An approved refund was already simulated as paid, and the result was saved.
The app restarts. The ledger still holds the earlier payout.
The user tries the same payout again. The payout checks the ledger and refuses.
